source.title: Quantitative W1 Convergence of Langevin-Like Stochastic Processes with Non-Convex Potential State-Dependent Noise
source.authors: Xiang Cheng; Dong Yin; P. Bartlett; Michael I. Jordan

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a full paper, though some equations and symbols are visibly garbled by extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper experimentally tests how SGD noise covariance relates to CIFAR-10 test accuracy, using covariance-matched injected noise as a conceptual test of a generalization mechanism. It does not test most claim versions directly.
record.gate_note: The paper reports CIFAR-10 test accuracy on models whose training accuracy is almost 100%, varying SGD step size, batch size and injected noise. These outcomes bear on V4's batch-size condition only insofar as they measure the version's test-performance relation; reported figures provide no exact values in the text. It does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, architecture comparisons, dropout, sharpness, or example removal. Cited claims and findings from prior work are not study results.
record.test_reason: The study measures CIFAR-10 test accuracy across batch sizes and learning rates with a common 2000-epoch budget. Its stated covariance trend implies worse accuracy at larger batches when learning rate is held fixed, and its noise-injection experiments test an adapted recipe. These results bear on V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially correct. The authors prove convergence results under stated assumptions and find empirically that noise covariance strongly predicts final test accuracy despite changes in higher noise moments. Similar test error for the limiting SDE remains a hypothesis, rather than an experimentally established result.
record.recipe_differences: Uses CIFAR-10 SGD noise-covariance sweeps and gradient-difference noise injection; measures final test accuracy, rather than directly testing large-batch generalization under fixed epoch budgets.
record.method_sensitivity: Final test accuracy varies with noise covariance; the text reports that, conditional on covariance, it is not significantly correlated with step size or minibatch size. Architecture differs between CNN and VGG19.

fits_no_version.finding: Across vanilla and noise-injected SGD, matching the covariance scalar predicts similar test accuracy despite different higher noise moments.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested CIFAR-10 networks near convergence, the SGD noise covariance scalar predicts test accuracy across learning rates, batch sizes, and gradient-difference noise injection.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 37th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 119, 2020
record.problems: Results are shown in plots without tabulated exact values or uncertainty estimates. Only two architectures and CIFAR-10 are tested. The runs use a fixed 2000-epoch schedule, but the paper does not compare large versus small batches under a fixed-epoch claim or identify a workload-dependent batch threshold.
record.rows_left_out: None. Rows R1–R6 capture the stated covariance and injected-noise test-accuracy outcomes for both architectures; exact plotted values are not recoverable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under different tuning recipes.
Language workloads, a quantified workload-dependent batch threshold, comparisons of training duration, warmup, and normalization or regularization changes.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap rankings, and comparisons with norm or margin measures.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for V5. Noise covariance here denotes a scalar multiplying the state-dependent gradient covariance, not a measured full covariance matrix. The absence of exact plotted accuracies prevents quantifying effect sizes, but does not prevent qualitative verdicts grounded in the authors' explicit statements.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-model comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and tuning or decay conditions.
No fixed-epoch large-batch comparison or workload-dependent threshold; the study varies batch size and step size for 2000 epochs and discusses test accuracy against noise covariance.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removing memorized examples and measuring test-accuracy effects.

rows.operation_detail: Measured final CIFAR-10 test accuracy across SGD step-size and minibatch-size combinations, plotted against noise covariance.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10
no batch normalization or dropout; constant step size

rows.measure: Final test accuracy versus noise covariance; text reports higher covariance leads to better final test accuracy and a linear trend with logarithm of covariance.
rows.note: Authors state training accuracies were almost 100% in most experiments. Figure does not provide extractable exact values in the supplied text.
rows.check: The direction is stated in Section 6.3.1 and Section 6: larger batches at fixed learning rate reduce the covariance scalar δ/b and worsen generalization. Exact accuracies are unavailable, but the qualitative effect is readable. The common 2000-epoch budget is a fixed-epoch comparison.

relationships.condition: Vanilla SGD on CIFAR-10 with CNN and VGG19, fixed learning rate and 2000 epochs
relationships.reason: R1 and R2 report better accuracy with larger δ/b; at fixed learning rate this means smaller batches generalize better, consistent with the authors' explicit batch-size interpretation.
relationships.display_finding: Unverified results suggest smaller batches improved accuracy at the fixed learning rate.

relationships.condition: CNN and VGG19 at batches 256 or 512 with injected gradient-difference noise
relationships.reason: R3 and R4 show improved accuracy after increasing covariance eightfold; R5 and R6 report accuracy similar to batch-128 SGD when its covariance is matched, supporting V5's recipe-adaptation qualification.
relationships.display_finding: Unverified results suggest that adding noise based on gradient differences improved accuracy. They also suggest that matching smaller-batch gradient covariance—how gradient components vary together—preserved comparable performance.
